KEY MESSAGE 1...Seasonable summer weather today with temperatures in 
the 70s to mid 80s, with seabreezes near the coasts.

Another great day of pleasant summer weather to open the 
workweek. High pressure near vicinity of Cleveland OH builds 
south, and brings a modest WSW to SW wind later in the day. 
Local seabreezes still look to develop, but full sun with highs 
in the upper 70s to mid 80s. A touch cooler along the coasts 
with the seabreezes. Clear skies continue tonight but we'll be 
starting to increase moist advection. There could be some patchy
mist or low clouds in interior portions of Southern New England
but probably not much impact.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Active weather Tuesday and Wednesday. Potential for 
hazardous marine conditions, high surf, soaking downpours and a
limited risk for severe weather.

As the aforementioned high pressure cell moves offshore, in its
wake is an approaching frontal system over the Great Lakes 
region with rather strong mid-upper level winds accompanying it.
Besides also leading to a tightening southerly pressure 
gradient, a southerly 925-850 mb jet upwards of 60 kt will 
permit strong moist advection and high IVT as PWATs rise to 
2.25" along the system's cold front/frontal occlusion Tue 
night/Wed. Several potential issues to Southern New England 
Tuesday into Wednesday. Ranked in order of highest to lowest 
confidence, these range from hazardous marine conditions/high 
surf, another round of soaking downpours, and a more limited 
risk for strong/severe thunderstorms potentially into the 
overnight hours. 

See the Marine portion for more details. Gale Watches have now 
been hoisted on most waters starting Tuesday afternoon through 
Wednesday early evening; multi-model-ensemble 34+ kt wind probs 
remain in the 50-75% range in the Gale Watch area, highest the 
further east/offshore one goes. The issue is on mixing in the 
southwesterly warm advection pattern, which those coarser-res 
ensembles can struggle to resolve, but potential exists for 
parts of or all of the Watch to see gusts into gale force range.
Although they're mostly wind waves in a southerly fetch, waves 
build to upwards of 12 ft and while not a beach day by any 
stretch of the imagination, the potential exists for high surf 
and later shifts will need to consider high surf or rip current 
headlines. Less common to see gale watches in the summer 
months, so hopefully getting the Watch out now conveys to 
mariners that conditions could turn hazardous especially Tuesday
night and into Wednesday when factoring in the winds and 
building rough seas. 

Showers and thunderstorms begin to increase Tuesday afternoon, 
and especially late in the day and into the Wednesday morning as
a combo of rising dewpoints and increasing upper support from 
being placed in the poleward exit region of a 70-kt 500 mb 
jetstreak provides additional upper support. Although severe 
weather potential looks quite a bit greater well to our west, 
increasing MUCAPEs and K- indices into the Tue overnight support
a risk for embedded stronger storms. Given the lower-level 
winds improve overnight, some risk for straight line wind damage
and/or a brief spin-up are possible, but would hinge on 
mustering enough 0-3 km CAPE. Wednesday might harbor a better 
chance at stronger daytime storms as the front will have moved 
offshore allowing for greater destabilization, and we'd be 
placed under the upper trough with still favorable mid/upper 
windfields. 

In terms of rainfall, it looks like areas along the southern CT, 
south coast and the Cape and Islands stand to see the most rain, at 
the expense of interior Southern New England. Ensemble 24-hr QPF 
probs paint moderately high (40-70%) probs of rain totals AOA 1 inch 
along the southern/southeast coast, and lower (< 40%) to the north 
and west. These areas have been getting quite a bit of rain lately, 
especially out over Cape Cod. But high FFG owing to the sandy 
soil could limit flooding. If we do get persistent downpours in 
some of our RI/southeast MA larger cities along a stalling 
frontal zone, then the risk would increase but this is 
uncertain. 

KEY MESSAGE 3...Drying out late-week with a return to more 
seasonable temperatures and lower humidity levels into next weekend.

Cold front stalls well offshore by Thurs, with an expansive high 
pressure across the Great Lakes ridging into the area late this week 
into the weekend. Temperature profiles are pretty cool for late 
July, at around +6 to +10C, but hard to get too cool with the sun 
angle being as high as it is. Thus expect seasonable temperatures, 
low humidity and dry weather late this week right through most of 
the weekend. Really not until Sunday when we get into a southerly 
return flow and with that comes increasing humidity levels.
